prompt: What is the purpose of the TCP three-way handshake?

options.text: To encrypt the connection by exchanging session keys before any data is sent
To synchronise sequence numbers and establish a connection before data transfer
To discover the server's IP address and confirm it is reachable on the network
To negotiate which destination port both sides will use for the rest of the connection

explanation: The handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) lets both sides agree on initial sequence numbers and confirm the connection is open. (a) Encryption and key exchange are TLS, a separate layer on top of TCP. (c) IP addresses are resolved by DNS before the handshake starts. (d) The client picks a source port and connects to a known destination port; no negotiation happens in the handshake.

prompt: How many round trips does the TCP handshake add before application data can flow?

options.text: Zero
One
Two
Three

explanation: SYN → SYN-ACK is one round trip. The client can send data with the third ACK, so the handshake costs one RTT. (a) Zero would mean no handshake. (c) and (d) overcount; the three segments travel in one round trip plus one one-way leg.

prompt: TCP guarantees that bytes arrive in order. What happens when a segment arrives out of order?

options.text: TCP delivers it to the application right away and leaves the reordering to the app
TCP discards it and waits for the sender to retransmit every segment after the gap
TCP buffers it until the missing earlier segment arrives, then delivers both in order
TCP treats it as a protocol error and resets the connection so both sides start over

explanation: TCP buffers out-of-order segments and delivers them to the application only after the gap is filled. (a) That is how UDP behaves (if the application chooses to reorder). (b) TCP does not drop correctly received segments; it buffers them and only the missing one is resent. (d) Out-of-order delivery is normal on the internet and does not cause a connection reset.

prompt: What does the TCP **receive window** control?

options.text: The rate the network path can carry packets before routers start dropping them
How many bytes the sender may have in flight before the receiver acknowledges
The maximum size of a single TCP segment that can be sent on the connection
The number of times a lost segment is retransmitted before the sender gives up

explanation: The receive window is flow control: the receiver tells the sender how much buffer space it has. The sender must not exceed it. (a) That describes congestion control, not flow control. (c) Segment size is determined by MSS (Maximum Segment Size). (d) Retransmission limits are a separate mechanism.

prompt: How does TCP congestion control differ from flow control?

options.text: Flow control protects the receiver's buffer; congestion control protects the network path
They are two names for one mechanism: the receive window that the receiver advertises
Congestion control is a UDP feature; TCP only needs flow control because it retransmits
Flow control runs at the network layer in routers; congestion control runs in TCP endpoints

explanation: Flow control (receive window) protects the receiver's buffer. Congestion control (congestion window) protects the network from being overloaded. Both limit how much the sender can send, but for different reasons. (b) They are distinct; the congestion window is the sender's own estimate, not something the receiver advertises. (c) Standard UDP has no congestion control. (d) Both operate at the transport layer, in the endpoints.

prompt: Which protocol does DNS primarily use, and why?

options.text: TCP, because a DNS answer must be reliable and a lost query would break every lookup
UDP: queries are small and skip the handshake; TCP is the fallback for large responses
Neither; DNS runs over its own dedicated transport protocol registered on port 53
TCP, because multi-record DNS answers need ordering guarantees to be reassembled

explanation: DNS queries and responses are typically small, so the overhead of a TCP handshake is unnecessary. UDP's connectionless nature also lets DNS servers handle more clients. TCP is used for zone transfers and responses that exceed ~512 bytes (or with EDNS, ~4096 bytes). (a) A lost UDP query is simply retried by the resolver after a timeout. (d) A typical answer fits in one datagram, so there is nothing to reorder. (c) Port 53 is used by standard UDP and TCP; there is no separate DNS transport.

scenario: A live video streaming service delivers 30 frames per second. A single frame's packet is lost on the network. The next frame arrives 33 ms later.
prompt: Should the protocol retransmit the lost frame?

options.text: Yes: every frame must be delivered, or the stream's quality drops for the rest of the session
No: a retransmission would arrive after the display has moved on, so show the next frame
Yes, but only after pausing playback so the lost frame can be shown before continuing
No: it should close the connection and reconnect so the stream restarts from a clean state

explanation: At 30 fps, each frame is relevant for ~33 ms. A retransmission takes at least one RTT. For most networks, that retransmitted frame arrives too late to display. Skipping it (or using error concealment) is better than freezing the stream. (a) Waiting for a late frame causes stutter, and one lost frame does not degrade the rest of the session. (c) Pausing playback is exactly the freeze users notice. (d) Reconnecting is far worse than dropping one frame.

scenario: An engineering team runs HTTP/2 over a single TCP connection to a backend service. Under 1% packet loss, they notice all concurrent request streams slow down together, even though only one stream's packet was lost.
prompt: What is this problem called, and what would fix it?

options.text: Connection pool exhaustion; opening more TCP connections removes the problem entirely
TCP-level head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes it with per-stream loss recovery
Flow-control stalls; raising the receive window lets the other streams keep flowing
HTTP-level head-of-line blocking; turning off HTTP/2 multiplexing would fix it

explanation: TCP enforces strict ordering across the entire connection. One lost packet blocks all streams until retransmission arrives: this is TCP-level HOL blocking. QUIC handles reliability per stream, so a loss in stream A does not block stream B. (a) More TCP connections mitigate but do not eliminate the problem and waste resources. (c) Flow control is about buffer space, not ordering. (d) HTTP/2 already removed HTTP-level HOL blocking; the stall here is in TCP, below HTTP.

scenario: A multiplayer game sends player position updates 60 times per second. Each update is 50 bytes. Players are on home internet connections with ~30 ms RTT.
prompt: Which transport protocol is the better fit?

options.text: TCP, because every position update must arrive reliably and in the order it was sent
UDP, because a stale position update is useless; the next update supersedes it
TCP with Nagle's algorithm enabled, so the small 50-byte updates are batched efficiently
Neither; real-time games bypass IP with a custom layer-2 protocol for lower latency

explanation: Position updates are superseded 16 ms later. Retransmitting a stale position wastes time and bandwidth. UDP lets the game send each update independently and discard anything outdated. (a) Reliable, ordered delivery adds latency for no benefit here, since a newer update replaces a lost one. (c) Nagle's algorithm batches small writes, adding delay: the opposite of what a real-time game needs. (d) Layer-2 protocols cannot cross the internet; games use standard UDP over IP.

prompt: Which of the following are provided by TCP but **not** by UDP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reliable delivery via retransmission
Checksum for detecting corruption
Strict byte-stream ordering
Built-in congestion control

explanation: TCP provides reliability (a), ordering (c) and congestion control (d). UDP does not. (b) Both TCP and UDP include a checksum field for detecting corruption, so this is not unique to TCP (though UDP's checksum is optional in IPv4).
